extractions.source_title: Grassy Shoot of Sugarcane | Pests & Diseases

affected_parts.evidence: Young leaves become pale in colour and appear thin and narrow. As the disease progresses, all new tillers grow in white or yellow colour, giving the plant a grassy appearance. The affected clumps are stunted with premature proliferation of auxillary buds. Secondary infection on full-grown canes shows side sprouting and yellowing. If canes are formed, they appear thin with shorter internodes, having aerial roots at the lower nodes.

summary.value: Narrow, pale leaves giving the plant a grassy appearance, with stunted tillers and premature proliferation of auxiliary buds. Infected full-grown canes show side sprouting, yellowing, thin canes with shorter internodes, and aerial roots at lower nodes.
summary.evidence: Young leaves become pale in colour and appear thin and narrow. As the disease progresses, all new tillers grow in white or yellow colour, giving the plant a grassy appearance. The affected clumps are stunted with premature proliferation of auxillary buds.

diagnostic_features.value: White or yellow colored new tillers giving a grassy appearance; thin canes with shorter internodes and aerial roots at lower nodes; papery and abnormally elongated buds on canes. Symptoms appear in random, isolated areas on the field, distinguishing it from iron deficiency which it resembles.
diagnostic_features.evidence: all new tillers grow in white or yellow colour, giving the plant a grassy appearance. If canes are formed, they appear thin with shorter internodes, having aerial roots at the lower nodes. The buds on such canes are usually papery and abnormally elongated. The symptoms have similarities with those of iron deficiency but appear in random, isolated areas on your field.

look_alikes.evidence: The symptoms have similarities with those of iron deficiency but appear in random, isolated areas on your field.

disease_name.evidence: The grassy shoot is a devastating disease that affects sugarcane, caused by phytoplasma.

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Sugarcane grassy shoot disease (SCGS), caused by ‘Candidatus Phytoplasma sacchari’, small, pleomorphic, pathogenic bacteria

type_of_disease.evidence: caused by ‘Candidatus Phytoplasma sacchari’, small, pleomorphic, pathogenic bacteria

affected_parts.evidence: The proliferation of vegetative buds at the base of the cane produces large groups of tillers with slender leaves. ... The phytoplasma infects the phloem tissue of the sugarcane plant, causing unusual tiller development and a reduction in internode length.

summary.value: Formation of abnormal tillers (grassy shoots) with excessive vegetative growth, reduced internode length, narrow pale green to chlorotic leaves, and stunted growth. Infected plants may produce up to 20 grassy shoots.
summary.evidence: The disease is characterized by the formation of abnormal tillers, known as grassy shoots, which are characterized by excessive vegetative growth, reduced internode length, and narrow leaves with a pale green coloration. Infected plants may produce up to 20 grassy shoots, reducing cane yield and quality.

diagnostic_features.value: Proliferation of vegetative buds at the base producing large groups of tillers with slender leaves ranging from pale yellow to completely chlorotic. Newly developing tillers are white or yellow. Thin canes with shortened internodes and papery, abnormally elongated buds. Stunted clusters with early proliferation of supplementary buds.
diagnostic_features.evidence: The proliferation of vegetative buds at the base of the cane produces large groups of tillers with slender leaves. leaves ranging from pale yellow to completely chlorotic on tillers ... All newly developing tillers are white or yellow, giving the plant a verdant appearance. Stunted clusters with an early proliferation of supplementary buds ... thin canes with shortened internodes and papery, abnormally elongated buds will be formed.

look_alikes.evidence: the symptoms can resemble those of iron deficiency, but only in random and isolated areas of the field

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Sugarcane rust is caused by Puccinia melanocephela, an obligate parasitic fungus.

type_of_disease.evidence: Sugarcane rust is caused by Puccinia melanocephela, an obligate parasitic fungus.

affected_parts.evidence: Sugarcane rust is mainly a disease of the leaf.

summary.value: Small elongated yellowish spots on leaves that turn brown to orange-brown or red-brown with chlorotic halos, developing into pustules mainly on the lower leaf surface that may coalesce into large necrotic areas.
summary.evidence: The earliest symptoms are small, elongated yellowish spots that are visible on both leaf surfaces. The spots increase in length, turn brown to orange-brown or red-brown in color, and develop a slight chlorotic halo.

diagnostic_features.value: Elongated lesions 2-10 mm long and 1-3 mm wide, brown to orange-brown or red-brown with chlorotic halos; pustules producing spores usually on lower leaf surface; infections most numerous toward the leaf tip, becoming less numerous toward the base.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Lesions typically range from 2-10 mm in length but occasionally reach 30 mm. They are seldom more than 1-3 mm in width. Infections are usually most numerous toward the leaf tip, becoming less numerous toward the base. Pustules, which produce spores, usually develop on the lower leaf surface.

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: The disease caused by sugarcane mosaic virus (SCMV) is commonly referred to "mosaic."

type_of_disease.evidence: The disease caused by sugarcane mosaic virus (SCMV)

affected_parts.evidence: Mosaic is identified primarily by its leaf symptoms.

summary.value: Contrasting shades of green on leaves with islands of normal green on a background of paler green or yellowish chlorotic areas, sometimes with leaf reddening or necrosis.
summary.evidence: The most distinctive symptom is a pattern of contrasting shades of green, often islands of normal green on a background of paler green or yellowish chlorotic areas on the leaf blade

diagnostic_features.value: Pattern of contrasting shades of green with islands of normal green on paler green or yellowish chlorotic background; chlorotic areas most evident at base of leaf; may also appear on leaf sheath but rarely on stalk; may be accompanied by leaf reddening or necrosis.
diagnostic_features.evidence: The most distinctive symptom is a pattern of contrasting shades of green, often islands of normal green on a background of paler green or yellowish chlorotic areas on the leaf blade (Figure 1). Generally, the chlorotic areas are diffuse, but they may be sharply defined in some clones infected with certain strains of the virus. The infection may be accompanied by varying degrees of leaf reddening or necrosis. Chlorotic areas are most evident at the base of the leaf.

affected_parts.evidence: Leaves become pale yellow to completely chlorotic, thin and narrow. The plants appear bushy and 'grass-like' due to reduction in the length of internodes premature and continuous tillering. The affected clumps are stunted with premature proliferation of auxillary buds. Cane formation rarely occurs in the affected clumps, if formed, thin with shorter internodes having aerial roots at the lower nodes. Two types of bodies are seen in ultrathin sections of phloem cells of infected plants.

summary.value: Numerous lanky tillers from base of affected shoots, leaves pale yellow to chlorotic, thin and narrow, plants appear bushy and grass-like due to shortened internodes and continuous tillering, clumps stunted.
summary.evidence: The disease is characterised by the production of numerous lanky tillers from the base of the affected shoots. Leaves become pale yellow to completely chlorotic, thin and narrow. The plants appear bushy and 'grass-like' due to reduction in the length of internodes premature and continuous tillering.

diagnostic_features.value: Production of numerous lanky tillers from the base giving a bushy grass-like appearance; leaves pale yellow to completely chlorotic, thin and narrow; shortened internodes with premature proliferation of axillary buds; canes if formed are thin with aerial roots at lower nodes and papery elongated buds.
diagnostic_features.evidence: The disease is characterised by the production of numerous lanky tillers from the base of the affected shoots. Leaves become pale yellow to completely chlorotic, thin and narrow. The plants appear bushy and 'grass-like' due to reduction in the length of internodes premature and continuous tillering. The affected clumps are stunted with premature proliferation of auxillary buds. Cane formation rarely occurs in the affected clumps, if formed, thin with shorter internodes having aerial roots at the lower nodes. The buds on such canes usually papery and abnormally elongated.

affected_parts.evidence: Chlorotic phase (chlorotic, rough, wrinkling, twisting and shortening of the leaves). Top rot phase (growing point is killed and the entire top of the plant dies). Knife cut phase (Its look like the tissues of the stem are removed with a sharp knife). Shortening of internodes.

summary.value: Disease progresses through three visual phases: chlorotic phase with leaf malformation, top rot phase where the growing point dies, and knife cut phase where stem tissues appear cleanly removed. Additional symptoms include shortened internodes and bud sprouting.
summary.evidence: Chlorotic phase (chlorotic, rough, wrinkling, twisting and shortening of the leaves). Top rot phase (growing point is killed and the entire top of the plant dies). Knife cut phase (Its look like the tissues of the stem are removed with a sharp knife). Shortening of internodes. Bud sprouting (it occurs during before maturation of crop).

diagnostic_features.value: Three distinct phases: chlorotic phase with wrinkling, twisting and shortening of leaves; top rot phase where the entire top of the plant dies; and knife cut phase where stem tissues look as if removed with a sharp knife. Also characterized by shortening of internodes and premature bud sprouting.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Chlorotic phase (chlorotic, rough, wrinkling, twisting and shortening of the leaves). Top rot phase (growing point is killed and the entire top of the plant dies). Knife cut phase (Its look like the tissues of the stem are removed with a sharp knife). Shortening of internodes. Bud sprouting (it occurs during before maturation of crop).

affected_parts.evidence: chlorotic patches towards the base of young leaves and occasionally on other parts of the leaf blades... transverse cuts in the rind of the stalk or stem... the apical parts of the stalks are seriously damaged

summary.value: Disease develops in three phases: chlorotic patches on young leaves, top rot with malformation and twisting of leaves, and knife cut stage with transverse cuts in the stalk rind.
summary.evidence: The disease develops in three major phases. The earliest symptoms are the appearance of chlorotic patches towards the base of young leaves and occasionally on other parts of the leaf blades in the first phase. Leaves are wrinkled, twisted and shortened.

diagnostic_features.value: Three distinct phases: (1) chlorotic patches at the base of young leaves with wrinkled, twisted, shortened leaves; (2) top rot phase with pronounced malformation, red specks dissolved, rotten and dried spindle base; (3) knife cut stage showing transverse cuts in the rind of the stalk, with large conspicuous chlorotic patches on stalks when leaves are stripped.
diagnostic_features.evidence: The top rot phase is the most serious stage where the malformation and twisting of leaves are pronounced. Red specks are dissolved and the whole base of the spindle gets rotten and dried up. In severe infections, buds sprout and the apical parts of the stalks are seriously damaged. The third stage known as the knife cut stage shows transverse cuts in the rind of the stalk or stem. When leaves are stripped off, large conspicuous chlorotic patches are seen on stalks.

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Sett rot or Pineapple disease - Ceratocystis paradoxa

type_of_disease.evidence: The fungus is soil-borne and enters through cut ends and proliferates rapidly in the parenchymatous tissues.

affected_parts.evidence: The disease primarily affects the setts usually two to three weeks after planning. The severely affected setts show internodal cavities covered with the mycelium and abundant spores. The setts may decay before the buds germinate or the shoots may die after reaching a height of about 6-12 inches. Infected shoots are stunted.

summary.value: Affected sett tissues develop a reddish colour turning brownish black, with internodal cavities covered with mycelium and spores, and a characteristic pineapple smell. Infected shoots are stunted and may die.
summary.evidence: The affected tissues first develop a reddish colour which turns to brownish black in the later stages. The severely affected setts show internodal cavities covered with the mycelium and abundant spores. A characteristic pineapple smell is associated with the rotting tissues. The setts may decay before the buds germinate or the shoots may die after reaching a height of about 6-12 inches. Infected shoots are stunted.

diagnostic_features.value: Characteristic pineapple smell associated with rotting tissues; tissues first reddish then brownish black; internodal cavities covered with mycelium and abundant spores.

affected_parts.evidence: Mature leaves develop longitudinal stripes or streaks... Infected canes are stunted with short internodes... The vascular bundles are deep red.

summary.value: Mature leaves develop pale yellow longitudinal stripes (3-7 mm wide) near veins and tips that later turn brown. Infected canes are stunted with short internodes giving a bushy appearance, and produce dull yellow bacterial ooze from cut ends with deep red vascular bundles.
summary.evidence: Mature leaves develop longitudinal stripes or streaks that are 3-7 mm in width and several centimeters in length. The stripes appear around the affected veins and near the tip. Initially the stripes are pale yellow in color and later turn brown. The affected tissues slowly dry up. Infected canes are stunted with short internodes giving them a bushy appearance. When stunted canes are cut, a dull yellow bacterial ooze (gum) comes out from the cut ends. The vascular bundles are deep red.

diagnostic_features.value: Longitudinal stripes 3-7 mm wide and several centimeters long around affected veins, initially pale yellow turning brown; stunted canes with bushy appearance due to short internodes; dull yellow bacterial ooze (gum) from cut ends; deep red vascular bundles.
diagnostic_features.evidence: The stripes appear around the affected veins and near the tip. Initially the stripes are pale yellow in color and later turn brown... The vascular bundles are deep red.

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: the bacterium Xanthomonas albilineans causes leaf scald

type_of_disease.evidence: the bacterium Xanthomonas albilineans causes leaf scald

affected_parts.evidence: a white line about 1–2 mm wide (also called a pencil line) on the leaf... Ultimately, the entire plant dies.

summary.value: White pencil line (1-2 mm wide) on leaf extending from midrib to margin parallel to veins, with diffuse yellow border. Disease progresses to brown necrosis from leaf tip or margin. Leaves look burned and curl inward, giving a scalded appearance, ultimately killing the entire plant.
summary.evidence: The most common symptom of leaf scald is a white line about 1–2 mm wide (also called a pencil line) on the leaf. This line extends from the midrib to the leaf margin running parallel to the veins. A diffuse yellow border of varying widths runs parallel to the pencil line... brown, dead tissue (necrosis) develops from the leaf tip or leaf margin and eventually extends the entire leaf. Leaves look burned and curl inward, giving them a scalded appearance... Ultimately, the entire plant dies.

diagnostic_features.value: White pencil line 1-2 mm wide extending from midrib to leaf margin parallel to veins; diffuse yellow border of varying widths parallel to pencil line; possible reddish discoloration along part of the pencil line; necrosis from leaf tip or margin; leaves look burned and curl inward.
diagnostic_features.evidence: a white line about 1–2 mm wide (also called a pencil line) on the leaf. This line extends from the midrib to the leaf margin running parallel to the veins. A diffuse yellow border of varying widths runs parallel to the pencil line. The pencil line may have areas of reddish discoloration along part of its length. As the disease progresses, brown, dead tissue (necrosis) develops from the leaf tip or leaf margin and eventually extends the entire leaf. Leaves look burned and curl inward, giving them a scalded appearance
